extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism and history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria and standards for American journalism around the Civil War and Reconstruction era as described in a history-of-journalism textbook chapter. Focus is on press role, ethics, editorial tactics, and failures of papers/editors in political engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press's proper role: represent the people, not control politics
rubrics_metrics.description: “The story of journalism now enters directly into the field of political reform. The question is no longer one of the newspaper in its proper field, representing the people, but of its controlling the machinery of politics.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats attempts by editors (Greeley, Raymond, Weed) to 'control' political machinery as a category mistake that led to failure; journalism ideally should represent public interest rather than seek direct control of political offices or machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Champion popular or moral causes
rubrics_metrics.description: “A journalist can never succeed unless he is fathering popular or moral causes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success for an editor/newspaper comes from leading or promoting causes that resonate morally or popularly. The book cites this as a practical rule explaining why some editors rose or fell with public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism should attack power, not serve in office
rubrics_metrics.description: “Great journalism is journalism in attack; great journalism is never journalism in office.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter argues that journalism's strength is oppositional and watchdog in nature; when newspapers or editors become part of the governing apparatus (i.e., 'in office'), they lose the capacity for effective journalism and often fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courageous independence and integrity of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Bowles: “A courageous independence and integrity of purpose, coupled with a fearless expression of truth as to all public individuals, corporations and parties, are the features in its character to be most encouraged.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press should cultivate independence from vested interests and speak truthfully about public figures, corporations and parties. This is presented as a normative character sketch for good journalism and a practical antidote to corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog duty: expose corruption and abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Press really seems to be the best, if not the only instrument, with which honest men can fight these enemies of order and integrity in government and security in property.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press is cast as the principal institution for rooting out political and business corruption. Examples: Samuel Bowles' denunciations of corrupt leaders and his exposure of James Fisk; sustained denunciation is presented as the press's reforming work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subserviency, indifference, or fear of prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have more to fear at present from its good nature, from its subserviency, from its indifference, from its fear to encounter prosecution and loss of patronage by the exposure of the wrong.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter warns against a timid or accommodating press that withholds criticism to avoid lawsuits, loss of patronage, or prosecution. Journalistic ‘good nature’ and deference are listed as present dangers that undermine the press's reforming role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify authenticity; avoid publishing forgeries
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of May 18, 1864: “the World and the Journal of Commerce printed the bogus proclamation of Joseph Howard, Jr. Both papers were immediately suspended…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete lesson: newspapers must verify documents and proclamations before publishing; failing to detect forgeries can lead to suspension, arrests, and loss of credibility. The incident is cited as a practical standard for editorial verification and fact-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bold editorial voice and rhetorical tactics to mobilize opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: the Tribune's “The Nation's War-Cry” ('Forward to Richmond!') and Greeley’s signed, heavily-leaded 'Prayer of Twenty Millions' — conspicuous, mandatory editorials printed in striking formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows that conspicuous editorial forms (large leads, capitals, signed multi-column editorials) can effectively mobilize public sentiment and press for action. It also cautions that forceful advocacy can have political costs (e.g., alienating policymakers or provoking rivals).
